notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for John 6:25–47, drawn from the sources accessed. Where a tradition or viewpoint could not be located in the fetched pages, it is not included.

---

**v. 25:** When they found Him on the other side of the sea, they asked Him, "Rabbi, when did You get here?"

- This exchange took place in the synagogue at Capernaum (cf. v. 59). The crowd is baffled: Jesus had not gone in the boat with the disciples, and no other boats had crossed except those they themselves used. Their question ("when" also implies "how") reflects natural curiosity about His seemingly impossible arrival. ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the difficulty of translating πότε ὧδε γέγονας — the "when" practically includes the "how." They suspected something linking Jesus to Moses, Joshua, or Elijah. ([Pulpit](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/6.htm))
- David Guzik (Enduring Word) adds that Jesus could have answered, "I walked over the Sea of Galilee in the night…then I miraculously transported our boat," but He deliberately refuses to satisfy their curiosity. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))

**v. 26:** Jesus replied, "Truly, truly, I tell you, it is not because you saw these signs that you are looking for Me, but because you ate the loaves and had your fill."

- Jesus ignores the surface question and exposes their motive. Ellicott explains: they had seen miracles but had not entered into their spiritual significance as "signs" pointing to His divine identity. They saw wonders but missed the truth to which the signs pointed. ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- The "Truly, truly" (ἀμὴν ἀμὴν) marks a solemn revelation. Jesus rebukes them: they came for more free food, not because they recognised Him as the spiritual Messiah. ([Pulpit](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/6.htm))
- John Piper (Desiring God, Baptist/Reformed-leaning) explains: the feeding was a "sign" — a beam of glory streaming from Jesus. But the crowd fixated on the product of the miracle (full stomachs), not the Person. "They were excited about bread as their pleasure, not Christ as their Treasure." ([Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/do-not-labor-for-the-food-that-perishes))
- Guzik notes that often we learn more from understanding why we ask God a question than from the answer itself. They wanted the bread plus a miracle-king to overthrow Rome. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))

**v. 27:** "Do not work for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you. For on Him God the Father has placed His seal of approval."

- The Greek is "work not" (present imperative), preserving a word-link with vv. 28–30. The contrast is not between working and not working, but between two kinds of labour: for perishable food vs. food that endures to eternal life. ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- "The Father has set His seal on Him": a seal was a mark of ownership and a guarantee of authenticity. God has certified Jesus as the authorised giver of eternal life. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))
- The Reformed reading (Ligonier): the crowd's quest for physical bread represents seeking Jesus only for temporal benefits. "To make obtaining it our chief end is a waste of time and effort." Jesus redirects them to the food that grants eternal life, which He alone can give. ([Ligonier](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-work-god-requires))
- Piper explains that the "labour" for eternal food is not meritorious work but faith (see v. 29). "The labour is faith. The labour is stop labouring. The labour is stop working and trust him." ([Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jesus-came-not-to-give-bread-but-to-be-bread))

**v. 28:** Then they inquired, "What must we do to perform the works of God?"

- The crowd picks up on Jesus' word "work" (ἐργάζεσθε). They ask, in effect, "What are the works God requires so that we may labour for this eternal food?" They think in terms of meritorious deeds. ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- Ligonier notes this reflects the Jewish belief that the Law is the bread God gives. They are asking which Mosaic works they must perform to gain eternal life. ([Ligonier](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jesus-bread-life))
- The StudyLight.org commentary notes: "It is in the human heart to think of salvation as a matter of 'works.'" ([StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/6-24.html))

**v. 29:** Jesus replied, "The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent."

- Jesus shifts from plural "works" (v. 28) to singular "work" — not an aggregate of deeds but a single, all-encompassing principle: faith. ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- Gill: "Faith is the chief work, and others are only acceptable when done in the faith of Christ. This, as a principle, is purely God's work; as it is an act…it is man's act." The object is Christ as sent by the Father. ([Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/6.htm))
- Guzik: "Jesus first and foremost commanded them (and us) not to do, but to trust. If we want to do the work of God, it begins with trusting Jesus." ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))
- Ligonier (Reformed): "Jesus called this a work inasmuch as belief is something that we do, but of course He did not mean that belief earns life eternal or that it is something we can work up on our own. It is a gift of grace, not a meritorious deed (Eph. 2:8–10)." Calvin is quoted: "Faith brings nothing to God, but, on the contrary, places man before God as empty and poor, that he may be filled with Christ." ([Ligonier](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-work-god-requires))

**vv. 30–31:** "What sign then will You perform, so that we may see it and believe You? What will You do? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written: 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat.'"

- Having just been fed miraculously, they now demand another sign as a credential — and they set the bar: Moses gave manna for forty years; Jesus gave only one meal. They subtly suggest Moses was greater. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))
- Ligonier notes: Jews in that day believed the Messiah would miraculously bring manna when He came. Jesus does not dispute this expectation but says their idea of life-giving manna is woefully inadequate. ([Ligonier](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jesus-bread-life))
- StudyLight: "So men are always willing to exalt Christ as a great personage, but are reluctant to receive Him as their Redeemer." ([StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/6-24.html))

**v. 32:** "Truly, truly, I tell you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven."

- Jesus makes two corrections: (1) Moses was not the ultimate giver — God the Father was; (2) the manna was not the "true" (i.e., ultimate, heavenly, spiritual) bread, merely a type. The true bread is now being given (present tense: "gives"). ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- Guzik paraphrases: "What other work will I do? This is the work: to give you the Word of God and eternal life in and through Me." ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))

**v. 33:** "For the bread of God is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world."

- The bread is identified as a Person: "He who comes down from heaven." Jesus is moving them from material bread to the spiritual reality — Himself. The scope is universal: "gives life to the world." ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))
- The Reformed commentary (Monergism excerpt) emphasises the present participle "comes down" — the incarnation is the ongoing source of life. ([Monergism search result](https://www.monergism.com/reformed-commentary-john-6))

**v. 34:** "Sir," they said, "give us this bread at all times."

- Like the Samaritan woman who misunderstood Jesus' offer of "living water" (John 4:15), the crowd takes the saying literally. They still think in terms of physical bread, albeit a perpetual supply. ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm); [Pulpit](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/6.htm))

**v. 35:** Jesus answered, "I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst."

- This is the first of the seven great "I AM" (ἐγώ εἰμι) sayings in John. Jesus identifies Himself as the bread that satisfies spiritual hunger and thirst absolutely and permanently. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))
- "Coming" and "believing" are parallel — coming to Jesus is believing in Him. The promise is comprehensive: "never hunger…never thirst." ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- Piper (Desiring God): "Jesus did not come into the world mainly to give bread, but to be bread." The satisfaction He offers is in Himself. ([Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jesus-came-not-to-give-bread-but-to-be-bread))

**v. 36:** "But as I stated, you have seen Me and still you do not believe."

- Jesus refers back to v. 26. They have seen Him with physical eyes — and even seen signs — yet they do not believe. Seeing is not believing; only the Father's drawing produces genuine faith (cf. v. 44). ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))
- This verse sets up the tension resolved in v. 37: the unbelief of many does not thwart God's plan, because those whom the Father gives will certainly come. ([Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/behold-believe-be-raised))

**v. 37:** "Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will never drive away."

- **Reformed reading (Calvinist):** This is a key text for the doctrines of unconditional election and irresistible grace. Those whom the Father has given to the Son (election) will certainly come (effectual calling). Jesus promises He will never cast out any who come — the doctrine of the perseverance/preservation of the saints. The security is absolute. ([Ligonier](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jesus-bread-life))
- **Arminian/Wesleyan reading:** The "giving" of the Father is based on foreknowledge; those whom God foreknows will believe are "given." The drawing (v. 44) is prevenient grace extended to all, which can be resisted. "Will come" expresses the Father's desire rather than an irresistible decree. (This was not directly found in the pages fetched; noted as a well-known difference.)
- Guzik (who writes from a broadly evangelical/charismatic perspective): this verse shows both divine sovereignty ("everyone the Father gives Me") and human responsibility ("the one who comes to Me"). The promise "I will never drive away" is absolute assurance for the believer. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))

**v. 38:** "For I have come down from heaven, not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me."

- Jesus explains the reason for His absolute commitment to receiving all whom the Father gives: He has come to accomplish the Father's will, not an independent agenda. This underscores His perfect submission and the unity of purpose between Father and Son. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))
- The Reformed commentary (Monergism) connects this to the covenant of redemption: the Son's mission is to fulfil the Father's decree of salvation for the elect. ([Monergism search result](https://www.monergism.com/reformed-commentary-john-6))

**v. 39:** "And this is the will of Him who sent Me, that I shall lose none of those He has given Me, but raise them up at the last day."

- The Father's will is twofold: (1) preservation — "lose none"; (2) resurrection — "raise them up at the last day." The security of the believer extends through death to bodily resurrection. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))
- The Reformed tradition sees here the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints: those truly given to Christ cannot be lost; Christ Himself guarantees their final salvation. ([Ligonier](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jesus-bread-life))

**v. 40:** "For it is My Father's will that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in Him shall have eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day."

- This verse restates v. 39 from the human side: "everyone who looks to the Son and believes." "Looking" (θεωρῶν) suggests a steady, beholding gaze of faith. The promise of resurrection is repeated, emphasising its certainty. ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- **Traditional reading:** Both divine sovereignty (v. 39) and human responsibility (v. 40) are held together. The Father's will embraces both the certainty that all the elect will be saved and the call for every person to look to Christ in faith. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))

**v. 41:** At this, the Jews began to grumble about Jesus because He had said, "I am the bread that came down from heaven."

- "The Jews" here likely refers to Judean pilgrims or religious leaders present in the synagogue, not the Galilean crowd. The verb "grumble" (ἐγόγγυζον) deliberately echoes the Israelites' grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:2, 7–8) — the very people whose fathers ate manna now grumble against the true Bread from heaven. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))

**v. 42:** They were asking, "Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then can He say, 'I have come down from heaven?'"

- The objection is based on Jesus' known human origins. They know His family; they assume natural parentage. His claim to heavenly origin seems to contradict ordinary experience. Ellicott notes they thought they knew His father (Joseph), unaware of the virgin birth. ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- Guzik: their stumbling block was familiarity. They knew the human Jesus too well to believe in the divine Christ. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))

**v. 43:** "Stop grumbling among yourselves," Jesus replied.

- Jesus commands them to cease their murmuring (present imperative: "stop grumbling"). He does not soften His claims to accommodate their offence. Instead, He presses deeper into the divine mystery. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))

**v. 44:** "No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day."

- **Reformed/Calvinist reading:** This is a key text for "irresistible grace" or "effectual calling." The Greek word ἑλκύσῃ ("draw") implies a powerful, effective dragging; it is used elsewhere of drawing a sword (John 18:10) or hauling a net of fish (John 21:6, 11). No one has the natural ability to come to Christ; the Father must sovereignly draw. All who are drawn will come and will be raised up. ([Ligonier](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jesus-bread-life))
- **Arminian/Wesleyan reading:** The drawing is God's prevenient grace, extended to all people through the Holy Spirit. This grace enables but does not compel; it restores the freedom to respond to the gospel, but the individual may still resist. (This distinction was not found in the fetched pages but is widely documented in Methodist/Wesleyan sources like Seedbed and Wesley's writings.)
- Guzik holds divine sovereignty and human responsibility together: "No one can come to Me unless the Father…draws him" emphasises God's initiative; yet the very next verse (v. 45) speaks of those who "have heard and learned from the Father," suggesting human response. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))

**v. 45:** "It is written in the Prophets: 'And they will all be taught by God.' Everyone who has heard the Father and learned from Him comes to Me—"

- The quotation is from Isaiah 54:13. The "all" refers to all who are in the new covenant community — those who hear and learn from the Father. The inward teaching of God is the means by which the Father draws people to the Son. ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- Guzik: this inner teaching does not bypass Scripture or preaching but makes them effective. Those who are "taught by God" recognise Jesus for who He truly is. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))

**v. 46:** "not that anyone has seen the Father except the One who is from God; only He has seen the Father."

- Lest anyone think the "hearing" and "learning" from the Father (v. 45) involves a direct vision of God, Jesus clarifies: no one has seen the Father except Himself — the One who is "from God" (παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ). He alone has immediate, direct knowledge of the Father. Our learning from the Father is mediated through the Son. ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- This verse reinforces Jesus' unique divine origin and authority, answering the objection of v. 42: they think they know where He comes from, but only He truly knows the Father. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))

**v. 47:** "Truly, truly, I tell you, he who believes has eternal life."

- The double "amen" signals climactic importance. Jesus declares that eternal life is not merely a future hope but a present possession for the one who believes: "has" (present tense) eternal life. ([Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/6.htm))
- This verse summarises the entire discourse up to this point: faith in Jesus is the sole condition for receiving eternal life. The "work of God" (v. 29) is to believe; the one who does so already possesses what the bread of life offers. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-6/))
- The Reformed commentary (Monergism excerpt) links this back to v. 40: the Father's will that everyone who sees the Son and believes should have eternal life is now being fulfilled in the present tense — "he who believes has eternal life." ([Monergism search result](https://www.monergism.com/reformed-commentary-john-6))

---

## Tradition Differences (summary from the sources)

**Faith and Works (v. 29):** All Protestant traditions agree that faith, not works of the Law, is the "work of God." The Reformed tradition (Ligonier, citing Calvin) stresses that even faith is a gift — "it is not a deed that merits a reward" but something we do when regenerated by the Spirit. Lutheran teaching would emphasise the law/gospel distinction: the crowd's question reflects the natural human impulse to seek righteousness by works, which Jesus redirects to the gospel of grace (this is a standard Lutheran reading, though no Lutheran-specific page was fetched).

**Divine Sovereignty and Human Responsibility (vv. 37–40, 44):** The sharpest divide is between Reformed/Calvinist and Arminian/Wesleyan readings. Reformed sources (Ligonier, Monergism) treat v. 37 ("all that the Father gives Me will come to Me") and v. 44 ("no one can come…unless the Father draws him") as teaching unconditional election, effectual calling, and the preservation of the saints. Arminian/Wesleyan traditions see the drawing as prevenient grace extended to all, which can be resisted, and understand the "giving" as based on divine foreknowledge of faith. Enduring Word holds the two in tension without strongly accenting either side.

**The Eucharist (vv. 48–58, beyond the requested passage):** Although outside the requested verses, the "bread of life" discourse culminates in language of eating Christ's flesh and drinking His blood. Catholic and Orthodox traditions read this sacramentally as referring to the Eucharist. Most Protestant commentaries (including Enduring Word) treat "eating and drinking" as a metaphor for receiving Christ's sacrificial death by faith, not primarily a reference to communion. (This was noted in the Enduring Word summary but not explored in detail for the requested verses.)
